I've noticed three groups of people reacting to the leaks: people who don't know anything about technology and are unphased, people who know a little about technology and are freaking out, and those that actually know how technology work and are mildly intrigued (but overall indifferent) by the data.

First group: technologically inept people

These people don't really know how their computers work, how networking works, and how COMPSEC works. They generally spend most of their time on social media, use Windows computers (because that's what the computer came with), and Skype with their family. Their trial of McAffee is still valid, and they'll use Norton when that's over. They download TurboTax and have toolbars in their browsers.

These are people who still get surprised when you tell them about a feature on their E-mail that they didn't know existed. They couldn't care less how security and encryption works, especially since encryption requires another password... and they probably don't have a login password on their computer, anyway.

This group (sadly) composes the vast majority of computer users.

Second group: HAKERZ!

These script-kiddies think they're 1337, and that they control the interwebz. They regularly claim to be part of Anonymous, and proudly show off their Guy Fawkes mask. They probably run Ubuntu or Mint, and they are just computer-savvy enough to hurt themselves.

They're called "script-kiddies" because the most advanced thing they're capable of is copying someone else's scripts/sketches and deploying them on some "target." If they were ever required to write anything of any real value, on their own, they'd outright to even try, because it's "below" their skill level.

These people share traits with group #1, in that they don't genuinely understand networking or COMPSEC/INFOSEC. Due to that, this leak has BLOWN THEIR MINDS!!! They can't believe how compromised their "secure" systems actually are, and they haven't shut up about it, yet.

This is the second smallest of the three groups, and that's a good thing.

Third group: the real keepers of the internet

These are the people that the script-kiddies leech off of. They actually know how the internet works, what to expect from it, and that no security is fool-proof. They understand that security is a deterrent, and a delay mechanism, and that if someone really wants in, it's just a matter of time... more-or-less time, depending on how much you've invested your knowledge into your system.

These are the people that are astounded by the leaks, and excited to get the information from them. These are the people that plan on reading through each exploit, and learning from it.

For instance: I found it surprising that the CIA didn't even try to break Signal, since they just interjected themselves between your software keyboard and the Signal app, and grabbed the data they needed before it was even encrypted.

These are the people that are awaiting the release of each and every one of the exploits: planning on taking advantage of business with weak/slow update/upgrade policies, people in the first group that won't update (ever), and script-kiddies who won't actually read the material in the leaks.

These people make up the smallest of the three groups (depending on your physical location), and they have remained largely silent about this whole thing... and for good reason. They knew that all of these platforms could be, or already were, compromised... they're more amazed at the ingenuity that was put forth in actually compromising the systems.

TL;DR: The only people that are vocal and surprised about this whole thing are the people that don't matter.

The Milgram experiment is a good reference here. It's a psychological experiment, but one that has been successfully replicated countless times more or less everywhere. It was meant to test peoples obedience to authority figures in reference mostly to the Nazis, but it's applicable to much more. In the original experiment people were put in a situation where they thought they were delivering increasingly powerful shocks to another participant in a setup where they could also hear the result of the other participant's increasingly desperate cries as a result of the shocks. In some variants the other person becomes completely nonresponsive as they approach the highest tiers of shocks.

The subjects were prodded on by the director of the experiment who would only 'allow' people to stop the shocks if they went through 4 tiers of increasing authority ('please continue, its required for you to continue, it's essential you continue, you must continue'). Most people thought nobody would go all the way to the max shock, which would almost certainly be fatal. In reality 65% did.

The point is that people seem to believe that if somebody in authority tells you to do something, even if it goes against every ethical notion in your bone - the vast majority of people will do so.
